Topic 01

General
Guidelines

Topic 01 — General Guidelines · 1 of 2

Position, Grip & Breathing

Body Position & Grip
Stable body position → safe alignment → proper stress on the target muscles.
Freestanding ground-based exercises → feet slightly wider than shoulder width.
Instability devices may need a modified position for stability.
Grip: usually a traditional grip from chapter 16, chosen by exercise demand.
Breathing & the Valsalva Maneuver
Exhale through the sticking point (concentric); inhale on the eccentric portion.
Structural exercises loading the axial skeleton may require breath holding.
≥80% MVC, or lighter loads to failure → Valsalva maneuver often unavoidable.
↑ Intra-abdominal pressure → ↑ spinal stability for lifts like the log clean.
Topic 01 — General Guidelines · 2 of 2

Guidelines Checklist

  • Position Proper alignment via a stable body position
  • Stance Freestanding, ground-based → feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, flat on the floor
  • Grip Use the appropriate grip for the exercise (see chapter 16)
  • Breathing Exhale on the concentric phase, inhale on the eccentric phase
  • Valsalva ≥80% MVC or sets to failure → Valsalva maneuver for spinal stability
Topic 01 — General Guidelines

Key Takeaway

Technique principles don't change with the tool — stable position, correct grip, and phase-matched breathing apply just the same to a kettlebell swing as a barbell squat.

Topic 02

Bodyweight
Training Methods

Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods · 1 of 5

Bodyweight Training

What It Is
Uses the athlete's own body mass as resistance.
Push-ups, pull-ups, chin-ups, sit-ups, squat thrusts — plus calisthenics, gymnastics, yoga.
Low-cost method that develops relative strength.
The Limitation
Resistance is capped at body weight → limited effect on absolute strength.
↑ Reps shifts the target from strength → strength endurance.
Fix: change the movement pattern (e.g. elevate the legs on a push-up) → ↑ resistance without ↑ reps.
Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods · 2 of 5

Benefits of Bodyweight Training

  • Specific Matches each athlete's own anthropometrics
  • Closed-Chain Engages multiple joints, strengthens several muscle groups at once
  • Relative Strength Develops strength relative to body mass
  • Control Improves body control and coordination
  • Versatile Can be done anywhere, at low cost
Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods · 3 of 5

Suspension Training

How It Works
Straps anchor overhead (rack, doorjamb, ceiling), hanging perpendicular to the floor.
Athlete manipulates their center of mass by hand or foot position → changes exercise intensity.
Strap Angle Controls Load
Steeper strap angle (center of mass closer to anchor) → higher % of body weight.
e.g. inverted row at 75° ≈ 79% body weight; at 30° ≈ 37% body weight.
A weighted vest can push the load beyond body weight.
Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods · 4 of 5

Suspension Training Benefits

  • Versatile Wide range of exercises targeting many muscle groups
  • Portable Easily transported, used indoors or outdoors
  • Space-Efficient Requires minimal storage space
  • Scalable Adjust difficulty via body position or strap angle
  • Balance & Coordination Challenges proprioception and body awareness
Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods · 5 of 5

Suspension Trainer Exercises

Inverted Row
Face the anchor, walk the feet forward, body rigid — leaning back loads the straps.
Pull the chest to the handles, elbows driving back.
Major muscles: latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, biceps.
Y-Pull
Lean back with arms extended in front at shoulder height, body straight.
Without flexing the elbows, push the hands overhead on a diagonal to form a "Y."
Major muscles: latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, trapezius, posterior deltoid.
Topic 02 — Bodyweight Training Methods

Key Takeaway

Suspension and bodyweight tools trade absolute load for versatility — the angle of the body, not an added plate, is what makes the exercise harder.

Topic 03

Core Stability &
Balance Training

Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training · 1 of 5

What Is the Core?

Anatomical Definition
Axial skeleton + all soft tissue with proximal attachments originating there.
Soft tissue = cartilage, ligaments, tendons, muscle, fascia.
Generates force (concentric) and resists motion (eccentric/isometric).
Its Job
Transfers torque and angular momentum through the kinetic chain (kicking, throwing).
↑ Core stability → better force-production foundation for the upper & lower extremities.
Linked to improved balance, throwing/hitting velocity & distance, and jump performance.
Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training · 2 of 5

Isolation vs Ground-Based Training

Isolation Exercises
e.g. prone plank, side plank — isolate core musculature without limb involvement.
↑ Muscle activation → may improve spinal stability, ↓ injury.
Limited evidence for transfer to sport performance in trained athletes.
Ground-Based Free Weight
Squat, deadlift, push press, snatch, rotation exercises.
Core activation similar to or greater than isolation work.
Strongest evidence for actual sport-performance transfer.
Isolation work helps most for athletes rehabbing an injury who can't yet load ground-based lifts.
Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training · 3 of 5

Machines vs Free Weight

Machine-Based
Added stability → better isolation of a target muscle, useful for hypertrophy.
Lower stabilizer activation than free weight (Smith machine squat: 30% less back-stabilizer activity vs free weight squat).
Free Weight, Ground-Based
Higher stabilizer muscle activation.
Offers the ideal combination of specificity + instability for strength & power development.
No need to add extra instability to a free-weight lift — it already provides enough.
Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training · 4 of 5

Instability Devices

What They Are
Unstable surfaces/devices originally popularized in physiotherapy rehab.
Swiss/physio/Pezzi balls, hemispherical balls, inflatable disks, wobble & balance boards, foam platforms.
Create postural disequilibrium → require core activation to stay upright.
The Trade-Off
↑ Instability → ↓ force-generating capacity of the agonist muscle.
Agonist force & power output can drop below 70% of stable-condition values.
Rate of force development is also significantly reduced.
Unstable-surface training produces muted performance gains vs stable-surface training.
Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training · 5 of 5

Core Stability Exercises

Stability Ball Rollout
Kneel, hands on ball, 90° at knees & ankles.
Extend the knees, flex the shoulders to roll the ball forward until near the face — hips stay rigid, no sagging.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas.
Stability Ball Pike
Quadruped, feet on the ball, elbows extended, torso rigid.
Flex the hips to roll the ball toward the chest until the hips are over the shoulders.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas.
Stability Ball Jackknife
Same setup as the pike.
Raise the hips slightly, then flex hips + knees to roll the ball forward until fully flexed.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas.
Topic 03 — Core Stability and Balance Training

Key Takeaway

Ground-based free weight training already builds the core — instability devices and isolation work are supplements for rehab and beginners, not replacements for the squat and the deadlift.

Topic 04

Chain-Supplemented
Exercises

Topic 04 — Chain-Supplemented Exercises · 1 of 2

Applying Chains

Method 1 — Chains Touch the Floor Throughout
Chains touch the floor through the entire extended range.
Produces a linear increase in resistance as the bar rises.
Method 2 — Chains Hang From Lighter Chains
Chains only touch the floor at the lowest point (bottom of the squat, chest level on the bench).
Full barbell-chain load applies only at the top, extended portion.
Result: heavier at lockout, lighter at the bottom — the resistance curve matches the body's own strength curve through the lift.
Topic 04 — Chain-Supplemented Exercises · 2 of 2

Why Chains Change Movement Velocity

Reduced Bottom Load
Links rest on the floor at the bottom → total load drops.
→ Athlete accelerates the bar faster off the bottom.
Within-Rep Potentiation
As chains pile on the floor and mass drops, neuromuscular activation may increase.
→ Possible within-repetition postactivation potentiation effect.
Faster Stretch-Shortening Cycle
Decreasing bottom load may cause eccentric unloading as chains pile up.
→ Quicker amortization phase transitioning eccentric to concentric.
Topic 04 — Chain-Supplemented Exercises

Key Takeaway

Chains turn a flat, constant load into a rising one — heaviest exactly where the lifter is strongest, at lockout.

Topic 05

Resistance
Band Exercises

Topic 05 — Resistance Band Exercises · 1 of 3

What the Research Shows

Supporting Evidence
Bands substituting 35% of back squat load → ≈13% acute increase in peak power (Wallace et al.).
Bands at 20% of load → acute ↑ in concentric rate of force development vs a constant load (Stevenson et al.).
Conflicting / Limited Evidence
Bands at 10% of squat load → no difference in EMG or ground reaction force (Ebben & Jensen).
Minimal longitudinal research → unclear whether acute effects translate to long-term strength/power gains.
Topic 05 — Resistance Band Exercises · 2 of 3

Band Mechanics

Tension = Stiffness (k) × Deformation (d)
Composition (thermoplastic/elastomer) sets stiffness → same-labeled bands can differ 3–5% in stiffness, producing up to a 19% swing in mean tension between "equal" bands.
Topic 05 — Resistance Band Exercises · 3 of 3

Applying Bands to Free Weight Lifts

Bottom Position
Bands are slack → no added tension → athlete lifts just the bar weight.
Top / Lockout Position
Bands are fully stretched → maximum added tension → total load is bar + band resistance.
To match a straight-weight load: average the band tension at top and bottom, then subtract it from the target bar load.
Topic 05 — Resistance Band Exercises

Key Takeaway

Bands do the same job as chains — building resistance toward lockout — but with band-to-band variability the coach has to account for.

Topic 06

Accentuated
Eccentric Loading

Topic 06 — Accentuated Eccentric Loading · 1 of 4

The Eccentric Strength Deficit

The Problem
Muscle is stronger eccentrically (lengthening) than concentrically (shortening) — up to 50% more force.
A constant load under-loads the eccentric phase relative to true eccentric capacity.
Under-loaded eccentric → ↓ motor unit recruitment & firing rate → ↓ stimulus for adaptation.
Topic 06 — Accentuated Eccentric Loading · 2 of 4

What Is AEL?

Definition
Extra load applied during the eccentric phase, removed for the concentric phase.
Typically delivered with a weight-releasing device.
Example
1RM bench = 120 kg → eccentric loaded at 100% (120 kg), concentric reduced to 60% (72 kg).
Jump example: hold + release dumbbells before the concentric (upward) phase of a countermovement jump.
Topic 06 — Accentuated Eccentric Loading · 3 of 4

Benefits of AEL

  • Mechanical Tension ↑ eccentric mechanical tension and eccentric work
  • Neuromuscular Improved voluntary muscle activation after 10 weeks of AEL training
  • Strength Gains Significantly greater maximal strength improvements vs traditional training in some studies
  • Architecture Possible fascicle elongation → higher shortening velocities
AEL hypertrophy gains match traditional training, not exceed it — the advantage shows up in strength and power, not muscle size.
Topic 06 — Accentuated Eccentric Loading · 4 of 4

Programming AEL

Submaximal
<100% of concentric 1RM as the eccentric load.
Maximal
100% of concentric 1RM as the eccentric load.
Supramaximal
>100% of concentric 1RM as the eccentric load.
AEL is an advanced tactic reserved for experienced lifters — match the eccentric load to the targeted outcome.
Topic 06 — Accentuated Eccentric Loading

Key Takeaway

The eccentric phase can handle more than the concentric phase can lift back — AEL is how you make training honor that difference.

Topic 07

Strongman &
Nontraditional
Implement Training

Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 1 of 8

Unique Demands, Unique Risks

Movement Variation
Farmer's walk, suitcase carry, yoke walk, tire flip, log lift, keg lift, stone lift — all drive high trunk/hip activation and spinal loads.
But each exercise loads the trunk & hip differently — variety builds broader spinal stability.
Injury Risk
213 surveyed strongman athletes flagged tire flip, yoke walk, and stone lift as the most dangerous.
Strongman athletes show higher injury rates than weightlifters, powerlifters, and bodybuilders.
Use loads that let the athlete keep control of their body and the implement — that's the real safety limiter here.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 2 of 8

Tire Flip

Setup & Injury
Three techniques: sumo, backlift, shoulders-against-the-tire.
Most common injury: biceps tears, usually from hands slipping.
Use dry tires with sufficient tread for grip.
Movement
Explosive triple extension of hips/knees/ankles drives the tire up and forward.
Push — don't lift — the tire over once it reaches hip height.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 3 of 8

Tire Flip — Flaws & Corrections

Feet Too Close
Flaw: rounds the back, knees crowd the chest.
Fix: move the feet back, brace the spine, drive up with triple extension.
Hips Rise First
Flaw: hips beat the shoulders up — the same fault seen in a bad deadlift.
Fix: keep the hips low, drive the tire forward, not up.
Lifting Instead of Pushing
Flaw: muscling the tire over loads the biceps and risks the tire falling back.
Fix: drive forward with the body, strike the tire with the quads at hip height.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 4 of 8

Log Lift & Weighted Carries

Log Lift
Essentially a clean + overhead press, performed with a metal log built for a neutral grip.
Three phases (first pull, transition, second pull) in two motions, with a pause at the shoulders.
Weighted Carries
Farmer's walk, suitcase (unilateral) carry, yoke walk, sandbag carry, Zercher carry.
Short, fast steps for balance early → longer steps, shorter ground contact as speed builds.
Heavy chest-loaded carries (Zercher, sandbag, keg) restrict breathing → may require bracing/breath-holding.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 5 of 8

Sled Training

Push, Pull & Drag
Forward push/pull — horizontal trunk & shin angle maximizes propulsive force.
Reverse drag — lean back, feet in front of the knees.
Research Findings
Loads of 5%–80% body mass improve acceleration (to ≈10 m) but not max-velocity sprinting.
66–75% body mass loads can produce a post-activation potentiation (PAPE) effect on 15 m sprint times.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 6 of 8

Kettlebell Training

The Evidence
Best-supported role: general physical/fitness development, not maximal strength.
6 weeks weightlifting: +13.6% squat, +4% vertical jump.
6 weeks kettlebell swings/goblet squats: +4.5% squat, +0.8% vertical jump.
The Verdict
Kettlebell swings improve cardiovascular fitness, but less than treadmill running.
Best used as general preparation — traditional weightlifting still wins for max strength & power.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 7 of 8

Kettlebell Types & Selection

Cast Iron vs Sport
Cast iron ("fitness") kettlebells vary in size with weight — cheaper, more common.
Sport/competition kettlebells: steel, fixed dimensions, weight shown by color.
Handle Matters
Fixed-load (cast iron/competition) vs adjustable (plate- or shot-loaded).
Polished steel handles hold chalk better and stay grippier than painted handles.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements · 8 of 8

Landmine Exercises

How It Works
One end of a barbell sits in a fixed cylinder or a wall corner; the bar becomes a lever around that point.
Loading the free end enables variable, multiplanar rotational resistance.
Common exercises: row, Romanian deadlift, squat, press, squat-to-press.
Popular in practice, but scientific research on the landmine's training effect is still limited.
Topic 07 — Strongman & Nontraditional Implements

Key Takeaway

Nontraditional implements test control as much as strength — technique discipline matters more here than it does with a barbell.

Topic 08

Unilateral
Training

Topic 08 — Unilateral Training · 1 of 2

Bilateral Deficit vs Bilateral Facilitation

Bilateral Deficit
Force output in a bilateral lift is less than the sum of each limb's unilateral output.
Seen in untrained, weaker, or injured athletes.
Bilateral Facilitation
Voluntary activation of the agonist increases during bilateral movement.
Seen in trained, stronger individuals.
Topic 08 — Unilateral Training · 2 of 2

When to Use Unilateral Training

Trained / Stronger Athletes
Show bilateral facilitation → bilateral lifts remain the primary strength-development tool.
Unilateral work (lunge, step-up, Bulgarian split squat) supports symmetry, not primary strength.
Untrained / Weaker / Injured Athletes
Show bilateral deficit → unilateral training can be genuinely useful for strength development.
Also serves as a rehab tool and a way to reduce bilateral asymmetries.
Topic 08 — Unilateral Training

Key Takeaway

Match the tool to the athlete: bilateral lifts build strength in the trained athlete; unilateral work rebuilds it in the untrained or injured one.

Topic 09

Exercise Technique
Library

Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Bodyweight · 1 of 5

Front Plank

Setup
Prone quadruped position, feet hip-width apart.
Palms flat under the shoulders, elbows pointed back.
Drop the elbows to the floor under the shoulders.
Step the feet back until the hips and legs extend.
Execution
Elevate the hips until ankles, knees, hips, shoulders, and head form a straight line.
Hold isometrically.
Elbows under the shoulders, head neutral.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, internal obliques, external obliques, erector spinae
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Bodyweight · 2 of 5

Side Plank

Setup
Lie on the left side.
Left elbow directly under the left shoulder, forearm perpendicular to the body.
Stack the right foot on the left (or place it just in front).
Stack the right arm on the torso, head neutral.
Execution
Elevate the hips until the ankle, knee, hip, and shoulder form a straight line.
Hold isometrically.
Then switch sides.
Muscles: internal obliques, external obliques
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Bodyweight · 3 of 5

Suspension Trainer Chest Press

Setup
Face away from the anchor.
Grasp the handles, elbows extended.
Hands and feet shoulder-width apart in a plank line.
Brace the trunk.
Step back until the straps are taut and the body is inclined.
Execution
Flex the elbows to lower the chest between the handles, like a push-up.
Extend the elbows to return to start.
Muscles: pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, rectus abdominis, internal obliques, external obliques, erector spinae
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Bodyweight · 4 of 5

Suspension Trainer Inverted Row

Setup
Face the anchor.
Grasp the handles (palms facing each other or up).
Lean back with arms extended in front at or above shoulder height.
Execution
Pull the torso to the hands by flexing the elbows and extending the shoulders.
Body stays straight throughout.
Extend the elbows to lower back to start.
Muscles: latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, biceps
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Bodyweight · 5 of 5

Suspension Trainer Y-Pull

Setup
Face the anchor.
Grasp the handles (palms facing each other).
Lean back with arms extended in front at or above shoulder height.
Execution
Without flexing the elbows, push the hands overhead on a diagonal to form a “Y.”
Body stays straight throughout.
Pause at the top.
Lower back to start.
Muscles: latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, trapezius, posterior deltoid
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Core Stability & Balance · 1 of 3

Stability Ball Rollout

Setup
Kneel facing the ball, upper body upright.
Elbows extended, hands on the ball.
Create a 90° angle at the knees and ankles.
Knees, hips, and shoulders in a near-vertical line.
Execution
Extend the knees and flex the shoulders to roll the ball forward until it's near the face.
Hold the torso rigid throughout.
Don't let the hips sag.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Core Stability & Balance · 2 of 3

Stability Ball Pike

Setup
Kneel in front of the ball, facing away.
Quadruped position — hands under the shoulders, knees extended, feet on the ball.
Hold the torso rigid.
Elbows extended, head neutral.
Execution
Upward: flex the hips to roll the ball toward the chest.
Continue until the toes are on top of the ball and the hips are over the shoulders.
Downward: return by extending the hips under control.
Keep the knees and elbows extended.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Core Stability & Balance · 3 of 3

Stability Ball Jackknife

Setup
Same setup as the pike.
Kneel facing away, quadruped, feet on the ball, torso rigid.
Execution
Forward: raise the hips slightly.
Flex the hips and knees to roll the ball toward the chest until fully flexed.
Backward: return by extending the hips and knees under control.
Keep the elbows extended.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, iliopsoas
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 1 of 7

Tire Flip

Setup
Face the tire, feet hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Squat and lean in so the chin and anterior deltoids rest on the tire.
Feet back enough for a neutral spine.
Grasp the tire with a supinated grip.
Arms outside the knees, elbows extended.
Execution
Extend the knees/hips and plantar flex the ankles.
Drive forward 2–3 explosive steps until the body is at a 45° angle to the tire.
Drive one knee up to strike the tire.
Switch to a pronated grip.
Push the tire over.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, soleus, gastrocnemius, deltoids, triceps brachii, trapezius
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 2 of 7

Log Clean and Press

Setup
Feet hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Squat down, hips lower than shoulders.
Grasp the log with a closed neutral grip, arms slightly outside the knees, elbows extended.
Neutral spine, scapulae depressed & retracted.
Shoulders over or slightly ahead of the log.
Execution
First pull: extend the hips/knees to lift the log, shoulders staying ahead of it.
Transition: as the log passes the knees, drop into a full squat and pull it onto the thighs.
Second pull: jump upward, extending the hips, knees, and ankles.
Catch: pull the body under the log and rack it across the clavicles and anterior deltoids.
Dip: drop to a quarter squat.
Drive: forcefully extend the hips, knees, and elbows to press the log overhead.
Lower it back to the shoulders, then the floor.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, deltoids, triceps brachii, trapezius
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 3 of 7

Yoke Walk

Setup
Adjust the yoke for ground clearance (≈4–6 in / 10–15 cm).
Bar on the upper traps, feet under the hips.
Hands on the vertical bars near lower chest height.
Execution
Brace the spine.
Push the feet into the ground while pushing the hands forward into the bars to stabilize the yoke.
Walk with short, fast steps initially.
Lengthen the stride and reduce ground contact time as speed builds.
To finish, flex the hips/knees/ankles to lower the frame under a braced spine.
Muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, gluteus maximus, rectus femoris, gluteus medius, erector spinae, internal and external obliques
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 4 of 7

Sandbag Carry

Setup
Position behind the center of the bag, similar to a deadlift stance.
Hook the fingers under each side of the bag.
Execution
Brace the spine.
Push the feet into the ground.
Row the bag into the chest.
Drop into a full squat as the bag reaches the chest.
Stand up via forceful hip extension to start the carry.
Walk with short, fast steps initially, lengthening the stride as speed builds.
Lean back slightly to offset the bag's forward position.
Muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, gluteus maximus, rectus femoris, gluteus medius, erector spinae, internal and external obliques
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 5 of 7

Zercher Carry

Setup
From boxes: bar racked on boxes.
Arms under/around the bar, palms up.
Bar resting on the inner elbows near the upper abdomen.
From the floor: overhand grip, semi-sumo deadlift to knee height.
Drop into a full squat and reposition the arms under the bar.
Execution
Push the feet into the ground and extend the hips/knees to standing.
Keep the bar on the inner elbows.
Walk with short, fast steps initially, lengthening the stride as speed builds.
Lean back slightly.
Muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, gluteus maximus, rectus femoris, gluteus medius, erector spinae, internal and external obliques
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 6 of 7

Forward Sled Push and Pull

Setup
Push: stand behind the sled, hands on the vertical bars between hip and knee height.
Heavy loads start feet together; lighter loads use a split stance.
Pull: stand in front of the sled, attached via harness or handles.
Trunk and shins close to horizontal.
Execution
Brace the spine and drive with short, fast steps initially.
Lengthen the stride and reduce ground contact time as speed builds.
Keep the front foot behind the hip throughout the pushing phase to maximize horizontal force.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, gastrocnemius, soleus
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Strongman · 7 of 7

Reverse Sled Drag

Setup
Face the sled, attached via a hip harness or handles.
Lean back slightly with hips extended, feet in front of the knees.
Heavy loads start with the feet together.
Execution
Drive backward with short, fast steps initially.
Lengthen the stride and reduce ground contact time as speed builds.
Keep the front foot in front of the knee throughout the pulling phase.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, gastrocnemius, soleus
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 1 of 9

Back Squat With Bands

Setup
Loop bands around rack pegs (or heavy dumbbells) and over the bar ends.
Slack at the bottom of the squat, tensioned as the bar rises.
Standard back squat setup: closed pronated grip, bar balanced on the back.
Feet shoulder-width or wider, erect torso.
Execution
Downward: flex the hips/knees under control, torso-to-floor angle constant.
Continue until the thighs are parallel to the floor.
Upward: extend the hips/knees to standing.
Torso erect, heels down, knees tracking over the feet.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris
Note: Bands should be slack at the bottom of the range — no load on the bar at the bottom of the squat.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 2 of 9

Accentuated Eccentrically Loaded Bench Press

Setup
Spotter loads the bar and attaches weight releasers.
Releasers set to disengage 2–4 in (5–10 cm) before the bottom of the descent.
Five-point body contact position.
Closed pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Bar over the chest, elbows extended.
Execution
Downward: lower the bar under control.
Releasers disengage before the bar reaches the chest.
Upward: push the bar up and slightly back as fast as possible to full elbow extension.
Keep five-point contact throughout.
Don't arch the back to meet the bar.
Muscles: pectoralis major, anterior deltoids, triceps brachii
Note: Spotting technique is identical to the standard bench press in chapter 16.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 3 of 9

Landmine Rotation

Setup
Grasp the free end of the barbell with both hands.
Press it up in front of the body at eye level.
Feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly flexed.
Weight on the balls of the feet, trunk braced.
Execution
Rotate the bar to one side, letting the torso, hips, and back foot rotate with it.
Forcefully rotate back to center, arms extended in front throughout.
Repeat to the opposite side.
Muscles: rectus abdominis, obliques, erector spinae
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 4 of 9

Single-Arm Landmine Row

Setup
Stand facing away from the pivot point, hip-width stance.
Working-side leg near the barbell.
Hinge at the hips (25–45° knee angle, 30–60° trunk lean).
Grasp the end of the bar, elbow extended.
Execution
Pull the bar up its natural arc by retracting the shoulder girdle, extending the shoulder, and flexing the elbow.
Continue until the bar reaches the torso.
Reverse the motion to lower back to start.
Trunk angle stays constant throughout.
Muscles: latissimus dorsi, trapezius, teres major, posterior deltoid, triceps brachii, rhomboids, brachioradialis, biceps brachii, brachialis
Note: Perform on both sides as part of a balanced program.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 5 of 9

Landmine Squat to Press

Setup
Face the pivot point with a slight forward lean.
Shoulder-width stance, knees slightly flexed.
Grasp the bar end 4–6 in (10–15 cm) from the shoulder with one hand.
Other arm out for balance.
Execution
Downward: flex the hips/knees under control, torso-to-floor angle constant.
Continue until the thighs are parallel to the floor.
Upward: extend the hips/knees to standing.
Press the bar up and slightly forward to full elbow extension as the legs finish extending.
Lower it back to the shoulder under control.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, deltoid (anterior, medial, posterior), trapezius, triceps brachii
Note: Perform on both sides as part of a balanced program.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 6 of 9

Two-Arm Kettlebell Swing

Setup
Straddle the kettlebell, feet hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Squat down and grasp it with a closed pronated grip, index fingers together, elbows extended.
Neutral spine, quarter-squat position.
Kettlebell hanging between the thighs.
Execution
Backward: flex at the hips to swing the kettlebell back between the legs until the torso is near parallel to the floor.
Forward/upward: extend the hips and knees to drive the kettlebell up to eye level, elbows extended.
Downward/backward: let the kettlebell drop, absorbing the load by flexing the hips and knees.
Then repeat.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 7 of 9

Single-Leg Squat

Setup
Grasp a barbell (or dumbbells for the variation).
Stand in front of a knee-height bench, one leg forward.
Instep of the back foot resting on the bench.
Both knees slightly flexed.
Torso nearly erect, shoulders back.
Execution
Downward: flex the hip/knee of the forward leg to lower the body vertically, torso-to-floor angle constant.
Continue until the front thigh is parallel to the floor.
Upward: extend the forward hip/knee to return to start.
Torso upright, forward knee over the forward foot.
Repeat, then switch legs.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis, rectus femoris
Note: Not typically spotted; if needed, two spotters flank the bar without touching it.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 8 of 9

Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift (RDL)

Setup
Grasp a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand.
Stand on the opposite (support) leg with the hips and shoulders over that foot.
Free foot staggered back.
Execution
Downward: flex the support knee slightly and hold it.
Flex the torso forward at the support hip, keeping shoulder-hip-knee-ankle in line.
Back neutral, elbow extended, until the torso and leg are parallel to the floor.
Upward: extend the support hip to return to start.
Don't hyperextend the torso or flex the elbow.
Repeat, then switch legs.
Muscles: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris
Note: Can be performed ipsilateral or contralateral — the contralateral version is described here.
Topic 09 — Exercise Technique Library · Other Alternative · 9 of 9

One-Arm Dumbbell Snatch

Setup
Straddle the dumbbell, feet hip- to shoulder-width apart.
Squat down, hips lower than shoulders.
Grasp it with a closed pronated grip, elbow extended.
Neutral or slightly arched back, chest up.
Shoulder over or slightly ahead of the dumbbell.
Execution
Pull: forcefully extend the knees, hips, and ankles to accelerate the dumbbell up the thigh.
Once fully extended, shrug hard and pull as high as possible.
Catch: pull the body under the dumbbell, rotating the arm around and under it while dropping to a quarter squat.
Extend the elbow to catch it in full extension.
Stand to fully erect.
Lower the dumbbell back to the floor in a controlled squat.
Muscles: rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, deltoids, trapezius
Chapter 17 — Recap · 1 of 2

Alternative Modes & Implements — Recap

✓
General Guidelines
Stable position, correct grip, phase-matched breathing, Valsalva when heavy.
✓
Bodyweight Training
Relative strength, low cost; suspension trainer angle controls load.
✓
Core Stability & Balance
Ground-based free weight beats isolation and instability work.
✓
Chain-Supplemented Exercises
Linear resistance rise toward lockout, faster bar speed off the bottom.
✓
Resistance Bands
Tension = stiffness × deformation; loads toward lockout, like chains.
Chapter 17 — Recap · 2 of 2

Alternative Modes & Implements — Recap

✓
Accentuated Eccentric Loading
Overload the eccentric, reduce the concentric — advanced athletes only.
✓
Strongman & Nontraditional Implements
Tire flip, log lift, carries, sled, kettlebell, landmine — control over load.
✓
Unilateral Training
Bilateral deficit vs facilitation decides who benefits most.

Every alternative mode in this chapter exists to solve a problem the barbell alone can't — match the tool to the athlete and the outcome, not the trend.
